So I don't seem to have understood this concept of a consolidated same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I should simply like to ask you, during the preparations for this trial it is not frequent that the witness can change something or add something to his preliminary statements. I don't see the difference in relation to this particular procedure. It is quite possible for something to be added to the consolidated statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know how you can call that statement a consolidated statement, then, because according to the previous explanation, a consolidated statement is compiled based on all previous statements and previous testimony. Then it's not a consolidated statement, then it's a completely new statement. Why should it be consolidated? What's being consolidated there? But I allow for the fact that perhaps I haven't understood it, so I won't take up more time with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the third question that I have tired you with quite a few times previously, but I promise you that I won't raise it again, but it has to do with finance. Yesterday I received a final letter from the Registrar concerning this issue, it was signed by Martin Petrov, the Head for Legal Assistance and Questions of Detention, it is dated the 4th of March, in which there are a few points I would like to quote and read out and that's where I'm going to end. Martin Petrov said that your ruling of the 30th of June, 2007, when you were the Pre-Trial Judge, that in it you made the conclusion that perhaps I do have the right for financial assistance by the International Tribunal for preparing my defence. And then three conditions are laid down which they say I have not fulfilled, whereas I have. I have proven that I'm indigent, that I can't meet the costs of my defence, and I appointed Slavko Jerkovic, as somebody who can be in charge of that question; although, he is not the main legal advisor who is Mr. Zoran Gazic, and you confirmed that. Next they say that legal assistance can be paid out in conformity with the rules and regulations, and they say that it is impossible to receive monies retroactively for the four years and several months until your ruling was made, and that the Registry is not bound to do so, that the situation is quite the contrary. And Martin Petrov goes on to say, I wish to mention that you never asked permission from the Registry with respect to any of -- any work concerning your so-called expert team, whereas for four years I struggled to have contacts with members of my expert team to be enabled to come and visit me, because for four years I wasn't allowed any visitors ever during that period of time, except once when I was represented with a chamber of the Netherlands in the Van der Spoel trial. Now, it appears that everything I do, expert opinions, reports, or whatever, I have to ask the Registry's agreement that that be done, although they did not recognise my legal advisors or didn't allow them to visit me or me to have telephone communication with them. Furthermore, the Registrar goes on to say that I did not want to supply them with information as to my family's property, and I don't wish to do so. I will never supply that information and I'm not duty-bound by any rules to do so. And he rejects providing information as to how much other defence cases cost and stand-by counsel and permanent counsel in my trial. They say that the sums were paid -- that the sums paid out to others in other trials are irrelevant as far as I'm concerned, and they refer to an Appeals Chamber decision in the Krajisnik trial, according to which the resources allegedly who are paid to the accused who represent themselves could not be comparable to those paid out to the Defence counsel and accused who have legal counsel to represent them, and that written matter is something that -- written statements is something that the accused representing themselves should compile themselves. And then they say that the Registry is ready to provide me with the total sum of the remuneration paid out to three Defence counsel that were imposed by the Tribunal but that it cannot and will not state the sums paid out to each individual Defence counsel because the secretary deems that information to be confidential, and it is only the Registry and the Defence counsel receiving those monies who know about it. So that is the final position taken by the Registry, Judges, so I'm not going to insist upon the matter further. You can give thought to the matter and see whether it will be possible for me to present my defence case under those conditions. Before the new year, my legal advisors and other members of my team warned me and said they will not be able to continue working much longer in this trial and help me in my defence unless they are paid, and I have that in writing, I have that caution issued by them in writing. I can bring it into court tomorrow if you're interested in seeing it. But I'm not going to discuss the matter or contact the Registry with respect to that issue until those two -- that information is supplied me, how much the other defence cases came to, how much money the Defence counsel received, and how much the individual counsels received from the International Tribunal. That must not be a secret. And I repeat my promise that I'm not going to abuse your patience with financial matters because I have put paid to that issue as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have the letter the Registrar sent to you and we know what you have just said, and we will address this matter. But you have said that as far as you're concerned the subject is closed. Let us bring in the witness now, please. The Prosecution has one hour and 37 or 33 minutes left, I'm not sure. Thirty-seven. That's an error on my part. Perhaps we could complete it today. I'm just going to ask him a question regarding the drafting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, "about the surrender."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "surrender." It's not the same thing. An error on the part of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before we give the floor to the Prosecution I have a question to put to you which is very simple: In the written statement that you signed on the 5th of March, 2008, in paragraph 19 you say that in Vukovar you heard the voice of Mr. Seselj calling on the Croats to surrender. When you mentioned this did you do so spontaneously yourself or was it the investigators who drew your attention to this particular point? Could you clear this up for us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I heard a voice that was similar to Mr. Seselj's voice. I said that spontaneously during the interview that I remembered this minor point. Well, minor point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you did not record this detail in the other statements that you made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, I didn't feel that to be that important at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Witness, how many persons in all were put in the buses? You said that there were five buses.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I made an estimate myself. If there were five buses, a bus can take 50 to 55 persons, roughly. So that's my calculation. Five times 50 is approximately 250 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. In your bus, what was the composition of the people? Were they men, women? Could you tell us that, the composition of the people on your bus?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They were mostly men, but I remembered later on that together with me in my bus there was a married couple. And apart from us there were two soldiers who were in front of the bus, in the front part of the bus by the front door, and of course the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I'll come back to this last part of your answer. Still talking about the composition of the people on your bus, could you tell us whether the people were patients, wounded men, invalids? What was their physical condition?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in my bus I saw people who had been wounded, and I saw people whom I couldn't say whether something had happened to them or not. But there were wounded people in my bus, too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you tell us the proportion of the people who were wounded in the bus?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: After all that passage of time I can try to remember. It was roughly 50/50, half/half. Of course that's not that reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Of course I understand. It's an approximation. Did you know certain people by name on your bus?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in my bus I recognised a member of my own brigade, not company but brigade. His surname was Gruber and I know that he had been wounded. His arm was bandaged. His shoulder, arm, and stomach had been bandaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you give us his first name?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Ivan Gruber. I know that Gruber was the surname. It's rather specific, but I think his first name was Ivan. Ivan Gruber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that there were two soldiers on the bus. Could you tell us whether they were JNA soldiers, or did they belong to some other group? Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It's like this: I'm certain that one of them belonged to the JNA. He was quite young and dressed as the JNA were dressed. As to the other one, I believe he was a little older and could have belonged to the reserve forces of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And what was their role in the bus? Why were they there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: At first I assumed on the basis of what I could see that it was sort of to provide security.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. You were all in the buses. Once you were in the buses what happened? Did you stay there? Did you move?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: For a time we waited in front of the hospital on the street there, and then after about half an hour to 45 minutes the buses started a manoeuvre and started moving. So after about 40 minutes the buses started driving off.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately what time it was when the buses started moving?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say that from the 9.00 I mentioned in the morning to the time they started moving, not more than -- well, it was not more than half past 10.00 or 11.00. 11.00 at the latest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. So you started off, as you just explained. Where were the buses going?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know this at the time, but sometime later we reached the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And how did you know that it was the barracks of Vukovar, the place where the buses drove to?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know at the time, although it was quite a specific place. You could notice that it was a military facility anyway. And later on I learnt that it was in fact the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When the five buses arrived at the Vukovar barracks, who did you see? Who was present?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There we came across the JNA soldiers, the territorials, Chetniks, in actual fact all types of the people we were fighting against, the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How many people were there in all? The JNA, the TO, and the Chetniks that you saw there, how many were they?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll try to hazard a guess. It's difficult to say and to give specific figures. There were a lot of them, I'd say. In that yard, in that compound, there might have been some 100 people. But as I say, it's difficult to give you an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Among this hundred or so people, had you seen any of them before?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: At the hospital I saw the same people that came up there to the barracks later on, or several of the same people. We all have to be aware of this fact that while we were driving in the bus we had to keep our heads down, so we couldn't really look around too much. But I did notice the same people at the hospital and at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And those same people that you noticed at the hospital and at the barracks, were they people belonging to the JNA, to the Chetniks, to the TO? Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, naturally there were JNA members. There were Chetniks too because the Chetniks were with us all the time. They were with the JNA and the Chetniks were behind us in their vehicles all the time. As far as I could see there were members of the Territorial Defence, too. There were Chetnik formations. There was the JNA who had organised and coordinated everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the attitude of the Chetniks when you were in the barracks in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll put it in my own words which perhaps won't be very grammatical but it was completely wild, completely savage. One could see that they wanted to take their revenge. There were verbal comments when we were entering the bus. You could see that they really wanted to harm us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You said that they made verbal comments, so can you be more precise? What did they say? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, you had the usual traditional swear-words that were used, the "swear-words" used in our lands. They would usually start with the words "Ustasha." So these were the usual swear-words. They would refer to your mother, to your homeland. They would call you an Ustasha and they would say that they would kill all of us, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What sort of frame of mind were you in in the bus? How did you feel?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were afraid. We were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What did the two soldiers who were in your bus do when the Chetniks wanted to enter the bus?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's quite clear that they were told not to let anyone in the bus, and they did not let one Chetnik get into the bus. So it seemed at that time that they were protecting us. As far as they are concerned, I can't complain about them behaving incorrectly towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did everyone stay on the bus or were there people who were taken off the bus?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No one was taken off my bus, apart from this married couple. I can't remember whether they were both Serbs or perhaps only the man was a Serb or the wife. But I think that they were well educated. They had a higher education. And as far as I can remember they were taken off the bus in Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And in the other buses, were you able to see anything in the other buses?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a JNA officer who would go into the buses with lists. He'd call out certain names. None of the names he called out were the names of people in our bus, but we could see that some people were taken off other buses if they were on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How many people were taken off the buses?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would be able to make an estimate on the basis of what I saw in this military bus that they put these people into. In my opinion there weren't more than about 20 people who were separated, at least in that bus. Naturally I couldn't see whether they took all the people into that bus, or rather, whether they put all the people into that bus, all of the people that had been taken off that bus had been put into the other bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know why these people were taken off the buses, what the criteria were for taking them off, what the reasons were?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What happened to them? Where were these people taken to?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think that bus was the last one to arrive in Ovcara. I must admit that I'm not quite clear about, whether I'm certain about this, given all the time that has passed. But I have a recollection, a vague recollection, of this bus following us to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. How much time did you spend in the Vukovar barracks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say that we stayed there for two hours at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And after two hours what happened?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say that this convoy of buses and other vehicles set off along a route that I was not familiar with, and we arrived at this location that we call Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you say "convoy," are you referring to the five buses, or did the sixth bus that you mentioned also form part of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember it went to Ovcara with us, that bus went to Ovcara with us, and it was part of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. How do you know you went to Ovcara? How do you know that the convoy arrived in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally at the time I didn't know that it was Ovcara, but at the time of being liberated from Ovcara and being freed, well, I was one of the local people - I'm from Zagreb - and it was the first time in my life that I was there. But from those people, those locals, I found out that the place was Ovcara, that it was a former farm and that it was Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What time was it when you arrived in Ovcara, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion it was around 1400 hours, perhaps 1430 hours. Perhaps a little earlier, but it was around 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: At that time were the two soldiers who were in your bus still in the bus or had they got off the bus?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They remained in the bus all the time, and when we got off the bus I think they even departed in those buses but I can't claim that for sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you describe the site you arrived at, Ovcara? What did you see, buildings, farms? What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can remember the building next to which we stopped, where the buses stopped. That's all I can remember. It was a big hangar. It had a large metal door. Perhaps -- it was perhaps 30 or 40 metres long, 15 to 20 metres wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. How did the buses park in relation to this hangar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the buses stopped parallel to the hangar, and the people who got off the buses -- well, the bus would arrive by the -- next to the metal door and that's where the people would get off. So the buses were parallel to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Which bus were you in when you arrived, in the first, second, third, fourth, fifth bus? Which one were you in?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the fourth bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When the bus you were in stopped, were you able to see what was happening outside, or was that only possible once you had got off the bus?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was possible to see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And what was happening outside? Could you describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the people who would get off the bus, they passed through -- they ran through a gauntlet in single file, a gauntlet composed of Chetniks. While they ran through this gauntlet the people would leave their personal items, their documents, and they would be beaten. After they had run through the gauntlet they would enter the Ovcara hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You mentioned the fact that there were -- that there was a gauntlet formed of Chetniks. The Chetniks who formed this gauntlet -- well, apart from the Chetniks who formed the gauntlet, did you notice any other soldiers who were part of any other groups, of the JNA or of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Look, the JNA was there all the time. They were constantly present. As far as I could see, they were in charge of the entire operation. So there was the JNA, the Chetniks, and the Territorial Defence members; they were always together on the whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. And with regard to the people who composed the gauntlet, did you recognise any individuals whom you had seen previously?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about my men or about the enemy? What are you asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I am referring to the enemy.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know any of them. They were practically the same people who had escorted us from the hospital, from the barracks as far as Ovcara. I had known them for two or three hours, but I hadn't previously known any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. How many people approximately were there who were beating you in this gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were about 20 to 25 individuals who composed the gauntlet, not more than that. Also because of the area that this was being done in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And could you tell us a little more about how you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They beat us with their hands, with rifle butts. One person even had chains. They would kick us. They would use anything they could get their hands on to beat us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How fast did the prisoners run the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that depends. Some would run through the gauntlet faster; some a little more slow. But it was between 20 to 30 seconds for each man. We ran through the gauntlet fairly rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And while you were being beaten, what did the soldiers who had escorted you in the bus do?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll repeat this: As far as I can remember the soldiers who were in the bus remained in the bus and the buses moved on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when the passengers in the buses were maltreated, the soldiers who were in the bus were no longer there; they had left with the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well because -- I'm putting this question to you because for us, the Judges, it's important to know who did what. Apparently, according to what you have said, there were three bodies in the field - the JNA, the Territorial Defence, and the Chetniks. You have said that the JNA was coordinating everything. That's what you said. And you have mentioned an event. You said that the buses left with JNA soldiers and there were individuals at the site, at the location you have described, that maltreated the detainees or those who had been on the buses. The Judges weren't present there. You are the victim. You were there and you are in the best position to tell us what happened. Did you feel that there was a change in the attitude of those who were guarding you there, or was their attitude the same as the attitude of those who had escorted you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll have to explain this in detail now. I'll need a little time to do so. Yes, in my head the situation is quite clear, but certain things can be confusing. When we refer to the soldiers who left that place, well, we're talking about perhaps 12 men who were JNA members and I wouldn't want this to confuse you. I don't want you to think that the JNA left that area. I said, I don't know how easy it is to interpret all of this, to make it understandable, but I said that the JNA coordinated the entire operation and that the three forces were still present in Ovcara. The soldiers who left the place constituted a small number of soldiers who were in the bus. In each bus there were probably about two men. So if we have six buses, that's 12 men at the most. So I hope I have been clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's very clear. Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Was it possible to avoid running the gauntlet, or did all the prisoners who were on the buses have to run through the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: They had to run the gauntlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you remember the names of some of the individuals who ran the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally I remember Ivan Gruber, who was with me on the bus. I also saw Zeljko Major. And I can remember two brothers who ran the gauntlet. I remember them from Vukovar but I can no longer remember their names. But there were a few people I recognised when they were running the gauntlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Once you got off the bus and before you ran the gauntlet composed of Chetniks who beat you, what happened?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I got off the bus. We lined up and we started approaching that gauntlet. At that point in time a soldier approached me. He started talking to me. On the whole they would ask us where we were from, they'd ask us what we were doing there, where we had fought. These were the usual questions put, and that is what I was asked about by this soldier. He asked me where I was from. I said that I was from Zagreb. And then he said something like, Well, what did you need this for? In two or three days' time I'll be leaving the army and going away to Ruma. And we established some kind of contact there. I told him that I had been in Ruma quite frequently. He asked me what I had done there. And then I told him that I had a very good friend in Ruma. He asked me who that friend was. I told him his identity. I asked him whether he could help me. He said, "That's not possible. May god help you." And then I said, "Save me if you can, please." However, it was time for me to run the gauntlet, and I ran the gauntlet, and then entered the Ovcara hangar itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a few other questions in relation to what you have just said. You said something about a friend. Could you give us his name?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Miroslav, also known as Kemo, from Ruma. I can't remember his surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. This soldier who addressed you, was he a Chetnik? Was he a JNA soldier, a reservist? Can you remember anything about this?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was a JNA soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Why do you claim that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he himself told me that he a few more days before he would complete his military service and that he was then going to Ruma. And given the way that he was dressed, you could see that he was a member of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you describe him for us? Could you describe his physical appearance?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time he was built like me. At the time I was -- I weighed between 70 and 75 kilos. He was about my height, 1 metre, 75. Short hair. Fairer than my hair, let's say light brown hair. And his face was a little narrow. It wasn't very long but it wasn't your usual round face.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. And as far as his clothes are concerned, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was dressed like a JNA soldier, but he had some kind of a JNA pilot jacket on him. He didn't have the usual JNA overcoat. He had a sort of spitfire pilot jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: As far as his trousers are concerned, could you describe them for us? Can you remember what sort of trousers he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I have said, everything else he had on him was the usual JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. After you had run the gauntlet composed of soldiers who beat you, you went to the hangar. And what happened there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after we had run the gauntlet we entered the hangar and they continued beating you there. There was another group of people who continued beating us there. Fortunately I wasn't beaten for very long in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I'll stop you there for a follow-up question. When you say that the beating continued, who beat you in the hangar? Could you tell us whether the Chetniks, the JNA soldiers, or members of the Territorial Defence beat you there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, the Chetniks were most active when it came to beating, but everyone would beat us. The JNA, the Territorial Defence, the Chetniks, everyone beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How many people beat you in total? Can you remember the number?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that in Ovcara, in front of the hangar and in the hangar, there were 150 men for sure. I know that there were more of them there -- they were more numerous than we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: My question was how many people were there in the hangar who were beating the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd say there were between 50 and 80 men who beat the prisoners in that hangar. I must admit that it's difficult for me to provide you with an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you describe how the prisoners were beaten?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not possible for me to describe this, but you could hear people's bones breaking as a result of the beating. They'd use iron rods, chains, rifle butts, spades, to beat the prisoners with. It's unimaginable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone you knew in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw Zeljko Major standing by the wall in the hangar. I recognised him. I heard them mentioning the name of Sinisa Glavasevic, too, and I assume that's the person who was lying on the ground and who was being beaten. That's what I can remember. But when you enter the hangar you're not really in the mood for looking around. It's difficult to remember the people who were there. I managed to remember these two individuals in the hangar, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the beating, as far as you are concerned, didn't last for very long. Could you tell us what happened, and why, when you say that it didn't last for very long?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I say the beating didn't last for long, I mean that it didn't last for more than two or three minutes. The others were beaten for two hours. I spent five minutes in the hangar at the most, because afterwards this soldier I had spoken to outside of the hangar entered the hangar and he spoke to an officer whom he called "Captain," and they both took me out of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly what he said to the captain whom you have mentioned, and how did you leave the hangar? Could you provide us with more details?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I entered the hangar. They started beating me. Three of them were beating me, I think. I was trying not to fall to the ground. I tried to duck my head to the extent that this was possible and then I heard someone say, "Don't beat him." I knew the voice. And this young man, this soldier approached me. They stopped beating me. This officer was with him. He grabbed me by the shoulder and he said, "Captain, let's save this man. I know him."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What did the captain say?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The captain then said, "Take him outside and make sure that the Chetniks don't kill him." After that he grabbed me by the shoulder, let's say he embraced me and said, "What's your name? I need to know your name." I told him what my name was. And as we left the hangar I stood by the door and I asked him what his name was. He then told me his name was Ilija and that they called him Stuka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: After that did you learn his first and last name? Were you able to establish who exactly he was?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: At the court in Belgrade I had occasion to hear his name, but even before that I came across his name in a magazine and then I saw that it wasn't Ilija but it was Stuka, which was still his nickname. And as far as I can remember this magazine - I don't know the name exactly - but it was published by the army, and Stuka was rewarded or decorated or something like that. I found this magazine in a garage in a location called Rakovica during the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And what was his full name indicated in the magazine?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, his full name and his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And what was it?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Spasoje Petkovic, Stuka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that he took you outside the hangar. Who was outside the hangar, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In front of the hangar there were another two or three men, some men that someone had saved. I can't remember exactly whether I was among the first to be taken out, but I know that there were some people already there in front of the hangar and that I -- and also I know that some people were brought to the same spot after me and saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In all how many people were taken out of the hangar and saved, as you say?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, today I know those names. Perko Faro ^, Cakalic, Guncevic, the late Perkovic, Kojic. Those are the names I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you say Perkovic, is it the same Perkovic as the commander of your unit that you mentioned at the beginning of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. It is the same surname. I even think they had the same first names, but they were two different people, another Perkovic that I didn't know from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What time was it when the seventh person of this group left the hangar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: All of us were taken out of the hangar roughly about the same time, within a period of some 15 or 20 minutes. However, we waited quite a long time in front of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How long did you wait in front of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In my assessment for at least half an hour. Maybe even as long as one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And who guarded you while you were outside?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this Stuka was next to me all the time and another soldier who was on good terms with him. I think they called him Mujidza or Mujidza. Mostly the two of them. And then another two of ordinary regular JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where were you waiting outside in relation to the hangar? Close to the hangar? Some distance from the hangar? Could you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It was in front of the hangar, right next to the entrance door, next to the wall adjoining the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In what position was the gate? Was it open, fully closed, half open?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: When we entered it was opened, but then afterwards it was half closed. They weren't fully open.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Were you able to hear what was happening inside?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I was. We could hear the beatings, the cries, the screams, the calls for help, yelling by the enemy, swear-words, bad language. In fact, I heard people's bones breaking while I was outside when they were being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier on that the beating lasted about two hours. I can check in the transcript. So this included the period you were outside while you could hear the blows. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, when I said two, maybe as long as two and a half hours, I'm talking about the entire period of beatings from the moment you ran through the gauntlet till you got inside. And the people who entered first they were beaten the longest, because the search and the running the gauntlet took a little time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. About what time do you believe that the beating inside stopped, in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they stopped, but again I didn't have a watch. But I can judge by the weather outside, by the fact that it was still daylight when the beating stopped. It just started to get dark when it stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the blows and the noise you heard in the hangar, did you hear other noises while you were outside the hangar that attracted your attention?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember some sort of a whistle like a football coach may use, a football referee, but it was some kind of a whistle used for orders and replacements because they couldn't go on beating all the time so they would probably taking turns. But I can't be very precise. I heard that whistle when I was in front of the hangar, and it's difficult for me to state clearly whether this was an indication of a change of shifts, but that is what I seem to recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. And outside the hangar did you hear any noises that drew your attention?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard some kind of a sound of some sort of a vehicle, a tank, a dredger. I heard the sound of an engine, some sort of engine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you ask what it was?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I did at a point in time. While I was talking about Stuka, I even asked him what was going to happen to all these people and he said they would be killed. Then I asked him what the noise was and then he said that they were dredgers digging holes. So that is what I learnt talking to him. I can't say that I saw any of that, but this is all on the basis of the conversation that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. What else did you talk about with Stuka when you were outside?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Stuka saw that I was wearing boots which they called Zenga, and these were boots, let's call them mountaineering boots or so-called Canadians that were manufactured in the Borovo footwear factory, and as it was getting colder the boots were very good for us because there were quite a number of boots in that factory. He suggested that I take off those boots, and I took them off so they wouldn't kill me as a Zenga because of those boots. And on a pile of footwear he found another pair of shoes. I put them on. And he also found an old leather jacket on this pile. He gave me that jacket too to put on. And I remember that he said that he had seen a ring on my finger, which I didn't take off when I got into the gauntlet. They took off my cross from the necklace, they took my documents, the photographs of my wife and child, but nobody took off my ring. And then he said to me, "It would be a good idea to take off that ring and throw it away so the Chetniks don't cut off your finger because of that ring." And I remember taking off the ring and I said, "Please, you take this ring of mine. It's better for you to wear it than for me to throw it into the rubbish." At first he didn't want to take the ring. I asked him, I begged him, I said, "Maybe one day you will be able to hand it back to me." It was my wedding ring. And after I asked him kindly he took it. And I remember that his hands were bigger than mine and he couldn't put it on his wedding finger. He put it on his small finger, on his little finger.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You said so as not to be killed because of these boots. Could you explain why the boots?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't popular for you to be recognised as a Zenga, as they called us. Zenga is short for ZNG which means Zbor Narodne Garde, or the National Guards Corps. And they had the impression that all the boots -- or, rather, whoever was wearing those boots was a member of the ZNG, the guards, though this did not correspond to the truth. They were simply warm and everyone used them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I understand. Did you at some point enter the hangar again?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. When the beating stopped, then they formed some sort of a group which was supposed to compile a list of names. And we entered the hangar. There was a small table there or some boxes or something like that, and JNA officers and soldiers were standing by this table and this is where they were making this list of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the situation in the hangar? What was the condition of the prisoners in there?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I didn't really look closely, but those that were close by and who I saw as I entered, I saw people lying on the ground. Some were still moaning and crying quietly. I saw some standing, too. I can't say whether those that were lying were dead or beaten up, but there were quite a number of people lying on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. After giving the names of the seven men what happened? Did you stay there? Did you leave?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We were taken out again in front of the hangar and a vehicle arrived. I think it was white. When I entered this vehicle I saw baskets that were used to distribute bread, loaves of bread, and then in this vehicle we were taken away from Ovcara. It was almost dark but not quite nighttime yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the exhibit under 65 ter 2521. 2521, page 21 -- 22, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, could you tell us what this picture shows?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I see now that it is the Ovcara hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, could you please assist the witness so he could mark with a circle the hangar that you entered and where the prisoners were put.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And would you mark it with the letter A.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: So a circle and the letter A.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell us where the five or six buses were parked and mark it with the letter B.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you now mark with a cross where you saw Stuka for the first time. Encircle this place and mark it with the letter C.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And perhaps you will need an arrow so as to avoid crowding, the spot where you waited outside together with these seven people, guarded by Stuka, make a circle and put the letter D there.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand where you want me to put an arrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: No, no, this is quite clear enough now. It's not overcrowded. So this is the spot where you were outside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to submit this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a number, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P276.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, perhaps it is time for the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are going to have a break. According to my reckoning you have used one hour, 50 minutes, so you will have another 40 minutes left when we resume. So we will now have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. We should be able to complete the examination-in-chief today. I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten seconds, please, just ten seconds of your time. Would you ask the Registry to provide you with a certificate that Marina Raguz has received the e-mail message, Marina Raguz. She says that the message arrived at 2005 hours last night and that she hadn't had an opportunity of confirming the reception of that message. That's what I learned in my telephone contacts. So could they provide you with proof that it was sent out on Friday, as they claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I don't have much time, Mr. Karlovic, so please listen carefully to my questions and answer very precisely. Once you left Ovcara with this group, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: From Ovcara we were driven first of all to Velepromet for a brief period and then we continued our journey to Modateks, the textile factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Who was present at Modateks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In Modateks there were civilians mostly - women, children, elderly person - and the JNA soldiers were there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What did Stuka and the soldiers who were accompanying you do once you arrived at Modateks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were with us throughout. They stood guard over us and handed us over at Modateks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Once they handed over -- handed you over to, I imagine, JNA soldiers, what did they do?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at one point I asked Stuka if he could stay with me until I was safe and he said he had to move on, and he left Modateks with the soldiers that brought us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened in the course of the night?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, during the night a group arrived at Modateks, a group of Chetniks, and they asked what we were doing there, why we were there, that we couldn't stay there and that they would come to fetch us in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Are you referring to this group of people that you were part of or to all the people who were there, including women and children?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the group that we were. Seven of us, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone from before amongst these Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I recognised one man from all these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the person who came to Modateks, I had seen him at the Vukovar barracks and at Ovcara, too, beforehand. He was perhaps a little taller than me. He had a moustache and the various Chetnik insignia - the cap, the cockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you learn his name?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, two names are in my head. I don't know how I remember those. So it's certainly one of those two names. Whether it was Topala or Budza.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you say "Topala" or "Budza," that concerns the Chetnik that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The name was Bulidza. Bulidza was the other name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: This person Topala or Bulidza, I apologise for my pronunciation, did this person say anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember that he asked us how come we were there, where we had come from, and then the locals from Vukovar explained where we were from. And at one point he said that he would kill us and those who had brought us there to that place, Modateks. And I still seem to remember that this man said -- I'm not quite sure, I think it was said in the morning, because after that night they returned in the morning to Modateks again and he said that he had been killing the whole night. So because of that context I seemed to remember that they said that when they returned on the second occasion. He said that he had been killing the whole night and that he would continue to do so and that he would kill us, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You said they came back in the morning so I conclude that you spent the night in Modateks. Did you leave with these Chetniks in the morning?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No. When they came in the morning at that place, Modateks, there was a group of soldiers there and a JNA reservist was in command of that group. I think his nickname was Deda. They referred to him as Deda, or grandfather, because he was a little older. And when they came to collect us in the morning, Deda told him that we had to clear up the whole hall and that afterwards we would be placed at their disposal, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Once you had cleaned up the hall what happened, when you had finished that work?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: When we cleaned it up, this man Deda organised some soldiers to get us away from that place, Modateks. So in a column, one by one, we moved towards Velepromet, which as far as I can remember was fairly near to this Modateks place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Why did they decide to send you to Velepromet? Why did Deda make this decision?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he even said that he was sending us there so that these people could come back and kill us. Deda seemed to me to be okay. His conduct was proper towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps repeat your answer? Perhaps there was a translation error. Did you say that he sent you there so that the others could return and beat you? Is that what he said? That's how it has been interpreted in English.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. What I was saying is that Deda took us over there so that they would not kill us, the Chetniks that came. And as I say, he wanted to get us away from these Chetniks who said they would kill us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. That's clear. When you arrived at Velepromet who was there? I'm referring to the enemy.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I saw the military police of the JNA. I saw the territorials, and they were the dominant people mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And you said that they were there mostly, but at Velepromet were there any other soldiers who were members of some other group, apart from the JNA and the military police?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, afterwards I came to realise that there were others, in view of the fact that the Chetnik units took people out of the premises we were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You have just mentioned the area you were kept in. You were placed in a building, in a certain -- at a certain site. Could you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's put it this way: It was a house or a warehouse. I don't know what to call it. I learnt later that they referred to it as the Stolarija, carpentry shop. Well, 50 or 60 metres away you come across that premises and they referred to it as the Stolarija, or carpentry workshop. And there was a door there and I entered and went left, because there were several rooms in that carpentry workshop, so I went left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How did you find out that it was the carpentry workshop? Did someone tell you that that was the case? Did you find out about it later?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I learnt that quite a long time afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And who told you about that?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't really know. I don't remember, but I think that when I was here to testify for the first or second time, I realised that it was the carpentry workshop. But at the time I didn't know that that was what it was. All I knew is that it was a house with those premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 65 ter 7182. 7182.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, while we are waiting for this next exhibit to come up on the screen, I would like you to explore with the witness because this is not entirely clear how many people were taken from Ovcara Farm to Velepromet and then to Modateks? Was it only the seven people who were taken outside and saved or did other prisoners come out of the hangar in Ovcara and brought along with them? So how big was the group that was taken away from Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know is that in my group, the group I was in, there were seven. Now, whether somebody else managed to escape or was saved afterwards, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you ever meet anyone from the farm at Ovcara again after you left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the people who were saved like me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. I did come across some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And did you meet some of those who were not saved with you outside, I mean any one of the other seven? Did you -- my question is: Did you ever see again any of the people who were left inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the photograph 7182. Could the Prosecution tell us where this photograph is from?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must admit that I don't know who took this photograph, nor do I know when it was taken. I'm only interested in the site, in the lie of the land, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Karlovic, what does the main building represent? What is it, the main building one can see in the middle of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That's the carpentry workshop that I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you take a marker and indicate, if possible, the place that you were detained in. Could you mark this location with an X perhaps.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to have this document entered into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P277, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Witness, how long did you stay in this location?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Several hours. At least three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Who else was there in that room?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: There were some other prisoners, people like me. There might have been as many as 20 people in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Tell us whether they were women, men, or children.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I remember the most being -- mostly being men. There was a young boy there, though, who was there who certainly wasn't older than 15. He might have been 13 or 14 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see people in uniforms or were they wearing civilian clothes? Could you describe how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The people in those premises were all wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And what were their ethnic origins?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I think most of them were Croats. But having mentioned that 14-year-old boy, as he was killed that day at Velepromet, later on his brother visited me in Zagreb when I was liberated and that's when I learnt that they were of mixed ethnicity. They weren't purely Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were in that room - and you already answered part of the question I was going to put to you - but while you were there what happened? Can you describe the events for us?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Chetniks entered the room, members of the Chetnik formations, and they would take people out, outside the room. I can't remember exactly now, but to the best of my recollections about three people were taken out before I myself was taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did these individuals go out together or separately? Were they taken out in a group or separately?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember they were taken out one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you remember who the first person to go out was?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The first person -- well, I can't remember exactly, but I do know -- I was 20 years old at the time so this man seemed to be older than me, and I would say he was about 40 years old, the man that was taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And did you find out about what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I did not find out, no. We could hear some of the initial conversation between the Chetniks and the people who were taken out, but all I know is that afterwards I learnt that all -- of all the people who were taken out, only I returned alive to the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. Can you remember who the second person to be taken out from the building by the Chetniks was?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I have to say that it's fairly difficult for me to remember all those things now and the order in which they took place. But I seem to remember that Perkovic was taken out, but I have to say that I'm not quite sure about that. And I do know that this young boy was taken out, the one I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And you said you could hear the beginning of a conversation between the Chetniks and the people who were being taken out. But did you hear anything else afterwards, once these three individuals had been taken out?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard when they said to this young boy that he should take off his clothes, and I heard when they started beating him and when he started crying and wailing and said, "Please, it hurts. Stop. Don't." And he was probably taken out, somewhere outside, so that the voices became feint. But we could hear something almost all the time. And some 10 to 15 minutes later after this moaning and wailing and crying, we heard some sort of shooting from an automatic pistol or something like that, we heard some shots, and that's where it ended. This noise or these screams stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you heard all of this? You were in a building and these individuals had been taken outside. How was it possible for you to hear what was happening once these people had been taken outside?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a window to that room and everything took place quite close by and with loud voices. But anyway, there was a window in the premises we were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you see any of these three people again after they had been taken out?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Just a detail I forgot to mention. The seven of you from your group were all in the same room, to the left, in the carpentry workshop. Is that the case? Or were you separated? Were you still in the same group in the room? And were these 20 individuals in that room?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: It's like this: As far as I can remember we weren't in -- all in that same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know where the others were, the others who were part of this group of seven?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that they were in one of the other rooms that existed there, because we could hear the voices from that other room. We heard the voices, for instance, when people were taken out of there. I heard them, actually. I heard them. I'm speaking about myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You said that you had been taken out. Can you tell us what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: As it was getting dusk, a group of Chetniks came to fetch me, a group that hadn't taken part in taking people out that day. There were three of them, actually, three men. And they said that I was being taken to the major for interrogation. But I knew that that was not the case. And they took me out. One of them held a rifle to me; the other had a Kalashnikov. And the man who was biggest built, Belgija, he held me and forced me to sing Croatian songs and took me from Velepromet along a road which was near the railway line, and some 100 metres on a vehicle arrived and we all got into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You mentioned a railway line. Was it far from Velepromet or close to Velepromet, the railway line where the car stopped and picked you up?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I exited by an exit on the opposite side and the railway was near Velepromet and the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Where did the vehicle take you to?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I was taken to Petrova Gora, to a house there where there were some Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How many Chetniks were there in this house?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say about 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Was this house far from Velepromet? How long did the trip take?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We weren't driven for a long time. It might have been just some two or three minutes until we arrived at the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find out the names of any of these Chetniks who were in the house?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: What I remember is Belgija, a man called Belgija, and some -- another man that they referred to as Cedo. And they had two names which I'm not quite sure of. The eldest Chetnik among them I think was Miljan or Smiljan, a name like that. And then there was a woman, and I'm not sure whether she was Darca or Arca, but something like that. So those are the names that ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How did you find out their names?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Belgija introduced himself to me and I heard other people calling this man Ceda and the other names. From them, I heard them referring to each other using those names. But Belgija introduced himself to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Once you had entered the house what happened?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as I entered the house there was general jubilation. Belgija spat in my face and -- well, can I use swear-words here, if you want me to repeat the exact words that were said to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Say what you remember, but it all depends on the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Say what you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when he spat in my face, he said, "We Chetniks will show you what we know. We're going to fuck your mother, you cunt."

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And after he said that, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: After that they made me sit down at the table, if I can call it that, somewhere in the middle of the room. The table was about 4 metres long. And all the Chetniks were sitting around that table. To my left there was Belgija; to my right there was this elderly Chetnik. I said his name was either Smiljan or Miljan, I can't remember. But behind me with a rifle to my head was Ceda. And the others were sitting around the table. Opposite me was this woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And how were you treated?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: The torture began straight away. They asked me where I was from, what I did. They kept beating me while they were asking me these questions. Then they took off the top part of my clothing and I was bare to the waist. They stripped me to the waist. And another thing that happened was I happened to be wearing a black T-shirt underneath my outer clothing and they said I was one of the black shirters, an Ustasha. They went mad when they saw this black T-shirt and the torture started up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Very briefly could you describe the kind of torture inflicted on you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the essential point to tell you is that when all this started there was somebody -- a man sitting in the corner of the room who said to -- asked them why they were doing all that, and they even had an argument over it. And after that Belgija told this man sitting in the corner, "If you don't want to take part, then leave the room," and the man actually did leave the house. Now, after that they tried to burn my hair with a lighter and my nipples, and they started -- they tried to set fire to my hair, but as it was damp at they didn't manage to burn me with the lighter. And there were two candles on the table, and then Belgija took one of these candles and placed the candles to my ear, to my hair, to my hand. And at one point because I wasn't tied, they hadn't tied me, I reacted instinctively and the candle fell off the floor -- fell off the table to the floor. And the person on my right went mad, took a bottle from the table, hit it against my head, cut my right arm and cut me on the back. And while I was still sitting on the chair, Belgija took up the candle again and started burning my nipples with this candle. I took it as long as I could and then I couldn't and started screaming and gesticulating with my hands. And then they started beating me again so I fell off the chair, fell to the floor. They started beating me again. They picked me up. However, at that point something happened. People entered the room, the people who actually saved me afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us how they saved you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: If I can just add something before I go on to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: During that torture the woman persuaded them -- tried to persuade them to rape me and then cut off my genitals and slaughter me in the yard, and she was persistent in that, in trying to persuade them to rape me. We can go on now. What was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes. That is your testimony and you are here to tell us. How did you feel? You said that two men entered. Could you tell us briefly what they did and how you emerged from this situation?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, two men entered, and later on I learnt who they were, but an argument broke out. The man whose nickname was Kinez, well, it appeared to me as he was some authority amongst these other people, and he said something like, "Belgija, why are you doing that? Did you capture that man at the front?" And I remember he said, "You're all young men. Why are you dirtying your hands with blood? There's been enough of all that. He's a prisoner of war. If he is guilty, he must be held responsible." But Belgija entreated him and he said, "We'll just do this one and then we won't do it anymore." However, this man Kinez did not give up. He went round the table, took hold of me by one arm, and with him escorting him was another man. I knew that he was a volunteer. I don't know whether he belonged to the Chetniks or the Territorial Defence, but I do know that he was a volunteer and his nickname was Mare and the two of them were armed and that's when the struggle started. They tried to pull me out of the house, and at one point they were successful. They did manage to pull me out of the house. They placed me in the yard. However, the Chetniks went of the house came into the yard again, and Cedo was the most aggressive one who had cocked his weapon at Kinez as well and this other man Maro, and Kinez said to him, "Brothers, don't force me to shoot. This is quite nonsensical. This mustn't go on." After that we went out into the street where, with my hands on up above of my head, I walked in front of them, several metres in front of them along the street and Mare and Kinez were escorting me that way. We entered another courtyard very quickly, and -- Am I speaking too fast? I'm sorry, am I too fast for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: In the courtyard, and it was already getting dark, somebody was waiting there for us. I think he was a captain. Anyway, he was an officer. And a woman was there, too. And they gave me some water to drink from the well and I was given an apple.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: After that where did you go?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to say is that Belgija came to the yard after me and he asked Kinez and Maro to hand me over to him once again. But they refused to do that, and that's important. Now, several metres away there was another house. We went into this other house which is where the military police was located. And there was an officer there belonging to the military police and he took me over. They gave me -- rather, I was given something to put on, some clothes, because I was bare. Anyway, this officer, Mare, Kinez, and two or three other soldiers from the military police, put me into an APC and they took me back to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. When you reached Velepromet where did they put you?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: I was taken back to the same room I was taken out of in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that room?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: As I was all bloody and cut up and I had wounds on my head, I was so tired that I sort of lost conscious -- I dropped off, I sort of went into a sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And you stayed there for a long time in that room, or did you go somewhere else afterwards?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: We stayed in that room, as far as I can remember, for about two hours, or perhaps one hour. And I do know that another officer entered the room. He was a man of short build, a sort of sports -- of a sports build with a strong voice. And while I was lying on the floor I heard him ask in Serbian, "Where's the man that they cut up?" And at first I was afraid but then I woke up, I came to, and I saw that it was a JNA army soldier and there was somebody else that seemed to me to be a special, one of the specials with a rifle and with a camouflage uniform, a security detail for that officer. He looked at my wounds, saw where I'd been cut up, and told a soldier who was standing there that he should go and fetch a doctor. And I remember him saying, "We've been fighting with the Ustashas for an hour and now we're going to have to tackle the Chetniks." After that, to cut a long story short, I was given medical aid and assistance and I was placed in that commander's car. And I remember this very well, it was an Opel Omega with a clock -- a little watch in front, or a clock. It's just a detail that I happen to remember. I remember looking at it and it was 20 minutes to midnight. So the soldier escorting this commander, whom I referred to as one of the specials, he sat -- got in the back of the Omega and he sat in the front with the driver of this Omega car --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll come back to that. Were other people following you also?

utterances.speaker: VILIM KARLOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I was going to say. To continue my story, while all this was going on and happening to me, the commander - and I realised that he came from the Vukovar barracks, I realised that later on - he organised everybody to leave the room.
